How would you structure ArgoCD Applicati: One ArgoCD Application per deployable service/environment combination is the default - it gives clean per-service sync status, health, and rollback rather than one giant Application whose status is meaningless when only one of ten services inside it is broken. Use ArgoCD Projects to group Applications by team or domain with scoped RBAC (which repos, clusters, and namespaces a team's Applications may touch), so teams get self-service control over their own Applications without needing cluster-admin-level access to ArgoCD itself.
How would you use the App of Apps patter: App of Apps uses a parent ArgoCD Application whose only job is to manage a folder of child Application manifests, so adding a new service is a Git commit adding one child manifest, not a manual ArgoCD UI action. ApplicationSets go further with a generator (a list, a Git directory glob, or a cluster list) that templates Applications automatically - e.g. one ApplicationSet generating one Application per cluster for a multi-cluster rollout, or one per directory in a monorepo of services - so the set of Applications stays in sync with the repo structure or cluster inventory without hand-maintaining each one.
How would you handle secrets in a GitOps: Never commit plaintext secrets - use either Sealed Secrets (secrets encrypted client-side, only decryptable by the controller in the target cluster, so the encrypted form is safe to commit) or the External Secrets Operator (the manifest references a secret by name in Secret Manager/Vault, and a controller syncs the real value into a Kubernetes Secret at apply time, so Git only ever holds a reference, never the value). Both keep the reconciliation fully GitOps-native - the secret's existence and reference are declared in Git - while keeping the actual sensitive value outside version control entirely.
What is the difference between ArgoCD's: Sync is the reconciliation action that makes the live cluster match Git - triggered manually, on a schedule, or automatically when Git changes (auto-sync). Self-heal is a separate setting that also reacts to drift in the other direction: if someone changes the live cluster directly (a manual kubectl edit) without touching Git, self-heal detects that drift and reverts the live state back to match Git even though Git itself never changed. Auto-sync alone would let manual live edits persist until the next Git-triggered sync; self-heal closes that gap by treating any live drift, not just Git changes, as something to reconcile away.
How would you design progressive deliver: Pair ArgoCD with Argo Rollouts (a CRD replacing Deployment) to get native canary/blue-green steps - shift a small traffic percentage, pause, run an analysis step querying Prometheus/Datadog for error rate and latency against the new version, then either proceed to the next traffic step or automatically abort and roll back if the analysis fails its threshold. The rollback trigger should be metric-based and automatic (error rate or latency regression crossing a defined threshold during the analysis window), not just 'someone noticed a problem,' so a bad canary is caught and reverted within minutes rather than riding out to full rollout.
How would you structure Git repositories: A common, scalable pattern is one manifests repo per team/domain (not per environment) with environment-specific overlays inside it (e.g. Kustomize base + dev/staging/prod overlays, or separate Helm values files per environment) - this keeps promotion between environments as a diff/PR within the same repo rather than a copy-paste across repos, while still giving teams independent ownership and blast-radius isolation from each other. A single company-wide monorepo can work at smaller scale but tends to need heavy RBAC/CODEOWNERS discipline to prevent one team's change from needing review by everyone, and to keep ArgoCD's per-Application sync scoped sanely as the repo grows.
An ArgoCD Application is stuck in 'OutOf: Check `argocd app diff` first to see the exact live-vs-desired difference ArgoCD sees, not just what a human diff of the YAML looks like - a common cause is a field a mutating webhook or the Kubernetes API server itself normalizes/defaults on apply (e.g. resource ordering, injected sidecar fields, or a controller like HPA overwriting replica count), which ArgoCD then perpetually sees as drift. If the diff is genuinely a field ArgoCD shouldn't own, configure an `ignoreDifferences` rule for that specific field/path rather than leaving the Application permanently and misleadingly marked OutOfSync, which trains people to ignore real drift alerts on that Application.
How would you promote a change from dev: Use a base configuration (Kustomize base or a shared Helm chart) with thin per-environment overlays that only override what actually differs (image tag, replica count, resource limits), so a promotion is bumping the image tag/values reference in the next environment's overlay via a PR, not duplicating the whole manifest. Automate the PR itself where possible (a bot opens the staging-bump PR automatically once dev's deploy is healthy, and a human approves it) so promotion is a fast, auditable Git-native action with a clear diff and approval trail rather than a manual copy-paste that risks drifting the environments apart.
How would you design a GitHub Actions wo: Use `paths` filters on the workflow trigger (or a dedicated changed-files action) to detect which service directories changed in the PR/push, then fan out to a matrix job or conditional jobs per service so an unrelated service's pipeline doesn't run at all. For a large monorepo, pair this with a dependency graph (if service A imports a shared library, a change to the library should trigger A's build too) rather than pure path-filtering alone, since naive path filtering misses cross-cutting changes to shared code.
How would you securely authenticate a Gi: Use Workload Identity Federation - GitHub Actions' OIDC token is exchanged for short-lived GCP credentials via a configured identity pool/provider trust relationship, scoped to a specific repo/branch, with no static key ever stored as a GitHub secret at all. This eliminates the biggest real-world risk with the key-based approach (a long-lived JSON key leaking from a misconfigured secret, a fork's workflow, or a compromised dependency) since there's no persistent credential to leak - only a token valid for the duration of that specific workflow run.
How would you cache dependencies in GitH: Key the cache on a hash of the lockfile (package-lock.json, poetry.lock, go.sum) rather than a static key, so any dependency change automatically invalidates the cache and forces a fresh install instead of silently reusing stale packages. Use `restore-keys` as a fallback for partial cache hits on a close-but-not-exact match (speeds up builds even when the lockfile changed slightly), but never cache build *output* artifacts across unrelated commits the same way - only cache genuinely reusable inputs like downloaded dependencies, not compiled results that should be freshly built per commit.
How would you design reusable GitHub Act: Composite actions bundle a fixed sequence of steps (e.g. 'checkout, setup language, run lint+test') into one reusable action referenced by tag/SHA from any repo, good for a self-contained step sequence. Reusable workflows (`workflow_call`) go further, letting one repo define an entire pipeline (build, test, security scan, deploy) that other repos' workflows call with `uses:` and pass inputs/secrets to, centralizing pipeline logic in one place so a fix or new security-scanning step gets adopted by every consuming repo through a version bump rather than copy-pasting YAML across dozens of repos.
How would you gate a GitHub Actions depl: Use GitHub Environments - configure the production environment with required reviewers, so any job targeting `environment: production` pauses and waits for an approval click before running, while dev/staging environments have no such protection rule and proceed automatically on every push. This also gives you environment-scoped secrets (production credentials only injectable into jobs targeting the production environment) and a clear audit log of who approved which production deployment and when.
A GitHub Actions workflow passes on ever: The most common cause is the PR workflow running against a merge of the PR branch with main automatically (GitHub's default `pull_request` trigger checks out a merge commit), which can mask a real conflict or missing dependency that only surfaces once the PR is actually merged for real - check whether CI is testing the true merge result or a stale/different ref. Other frequent causes: environment or secret differences between the PR context (forked PRs often can't access repo secrets at all, for security) and the main-branch job, or a race/flaky test that happened to pass by chance on the PR run - re-run main's failing job first to rule out flakiness before assuming it's environmental.
How would you control GitHub Actions run: Use `concurrency` groups keyed on the branch/PR so a new push to the same PR cancels the previous in-flight run instead of both running to completion, which is usually the single biggest cost/queue-time win for active PRs with frequent pushes. Scope expensive jobs (full test suites, deploys) to only run on paths that matter or only after a lighter required check passes, use self-hosted runners with autoscaling for high-volume workloads instead of paying per-minute for GitHub-hosted runners at scale, and set workflow-level timeouts so a hung job doesn't silently burn runner-minutes for hours.
How would you design a Jenkins Shared Li: Build a versioned Shared Library repo with reusable steps (`vars/*.groovy` for simple callable steps, `src/` for more structured classes) covering common stages - build, test, security scan, deploy - and have each team's Jenkinsfile load a specific tagged version (`@Library('common-pipeline@v2.1')`) rather than `@latest`, so a library change doesn't silently break every consuming pipeline the moment it merges. Treat the library itself like a product with its own tests and semantic versioning, since dozens of teams' CI now depends on it working correctly.
In a Jenkins multibranch pipeline, how w: Use a `when { branch 'main' }` or `when { changeRequest() }` directive on the specific stage in the Jenkinsfile - Jenkins evaluates this per-run using the branch/PR context the multibranch job already knows, so the same Jenkinsfile can run a full deploy stage only on main while running build+test (but skipping deploy) on every feature branch and PR automatically, without needing separate Jenkinsfiles per branch type.
How would you handle Jenkins agent/execu: Use cloud-based ephemeral agents (Kubernetes plugin spinning up a pod per build) instead of a fixed pool of static agents, so executor capacity scales with actual PR volume rather than being capped by however many static agents happen to be provisioned. Where capacity truly is fixed, use label-based agent pools and `throttle` /concurrency limits so multibranch PR builds are confined to their own pool and can't consume every executor a critical scheduled job (like a nightly deploy or security scan) also needs.
How would you clean up orphaned Jenkins: Enable the multibranch pipeline's built-in orphaned item strategy (Scan Multibranch Pipeline Triggers -> 'Discard old items' with a retention period), which automatically removes the Jenkins job for a branch once its source branch/PR no longer exists upstream, rather than letting deleted branches accumulate as stale jobs forever. Pair this with a periodic branch-source re-scan (webhook-triggered plus a periodic fallback scan) so deletions are actually detected promptly instead of only being noticed the next time someone manually triggers a rescan.
How would you pass secrets into a Jenkin: Store secrets only in the Jenkins Credentials store (never in the Jenkinsfile or repo) and inject them via `withCredentials` scoped to the specific step that needs them, masked automatically from logs. Critically, treat PRs from forks as untrusted code - Jenkins' GitHub Branch Source plugin has settings to restrict whether fork PRs can even trigger builds, and if they can, ensure credential-requiring stages (deploy, publish) are gated behind `when { not { changeRequest() } }` or a trusted-branch check, since a malicious fork PR's Jenkinsfile could otherwise attempt to exfiltrate any secret it's given access to.
How would you version and test changes t: Since the multibranch job already runs whatever Jenkinsfile is on each branch, a PR changing the Jenkinsfile gets tested automatically on that PR's own branch before merge - the practical discipline is making sure the PR's pipeline run is a required status check before merge, so a syntactically broken or logically wrong Jenkinsfile change fails visibly on the PR rather than silently landing on main and breaking CI for everyone. For larger changes (e.g. a Shared Library upgrade), test against a throwaway branch first and treat the Jenkinsfile with the same PR-review rigor as production code, since in practice it is.
A specific branch's Jenkins multibranch: Check the trigger configuration first - a webhook misconfigured to fire on unrelated events (e.g. every push to any branch triggering a rescan of all branches, or a status-check webhook loop where Jenkins posting a commit status back to GitHub itself triggers another webhook) is the most common cause. Also check for a periodic 'Scan Multibranch Pipeline Triggers' interval set too aggressively combined with `Build Strategies` set to build on every scan regardless of whether the branch's actual head SHA changed - tightening the build strategy to only build on new SHA changes (not just 'branch exists') usually stops the loop.
